titleZh: 蒙大拿州经济发展峰会
summaryEn: Keynote address on SpaceX, Tesla and sustainable energy at the Montana Jobs Summit in Butte.
summaryZh: 在比尤特举行的蒙大拿州就业峰会上发表关于 SpaceX、Tesla 和可持续能源的主题演讲。

segments.textEn: Next speaker certainly thinks big, very big. He dreams big, does big things. His ideas have been described as excessively
segments.textZh: 下一位演讲者的想法无疑很宏大，非常宏大。他有远大的梦想，做大事。他的想法被形容为过分地

segments.textEn: cool
segments.textZh: 酷

segments.textEn: whether it's PayPal the car or SpaceX obviously as you know when the co founders of PayPal CEO today, Tesla drove one of his cars a short while ago and man they are, they got pick up and cool. They are really cool.
segments.textZh: 无论是 PayPal、汽车还是 SpaceX，显然，正如各位所知，当 PayPal 的联合创始人、如今的首席执行官，Tesla，不久前驾驶过他的一辆车，天啊，它们，它们加速很猛，而且很酷。它们真的很酷。

segments.textEn: SpaceX, you know, he's tied in here with Seacast because a lot of SpaceX rocket components are made right here in Butte by the Robins family. So we're very, very proud of all that. Let's give a big, big round of applause to Elon Musk.
segments.textZh: SpaceX，你们知道，他通过 Seacast 与这里建立了联系，因为许多 SpaceX 火箭部件正是由罗宾斯家族在比尤特这里制造的。所以我们对此感到非常、非常自豪。让我们用非常、非常热烈的掌声欢迎埃隆·马斯克。

segments.textEn: All right, thanks very much for having me. I actually just came from ccast which
segments.textZh: 好的，非常感谢你们邀请我。其实我刚从 ccast 过来，那里

segments.textEn: is
segments.textZh: 是

segments.textEn: they make cast titanium and inconel parts for the SpaceX rocket engines and actually brought all my five kids who are sitting right there.
segments.textZh: 他们为 SpaceX 火箭发动机制造铸钛和铬镍铁合金零件，而且实际上我把我的5个孩子都带来了，他们就坐在那里。

segments.textEn: So they got to see steel being poured and then titanium being poured as well and creating sophisticated castings. They seem pretty excited about that. And it was kind of like Charlie and the metal factory I guess.
segments.textZh: 所以他们看到了钢水浇注，之后也看到了钛液浇注并制成复杂的铸件。他们似乎对此相当兴奋。我猜这有点像《查理和金属工厂》。

segments.textEn: So let's see. I guess I'll maybe talk a bit about entrepreneurship and technology, tell you about my experiences and what happened to me and then I think we're going to try to reserve as much time as possible for Q and A from the audience and certainly feel free to ask any questions, any and every question.
segments.textZh: 那么，让我想想。我想我可能会谈一点创业和技术，跟各位讲讲我的经历以及发生在我身上的事，然后我想我们会尽量为现场观众的问答留出尽可能多的时间，当然，大家尽管提出任何问题，任何一个、每一个问题都可以。

segments.textEn: And so I'll kind of give the nutshell account because it's getting a little bit long at this point. So I arrived in North America when I was about 17. I was born in South Africa, but I was actually named after my American great grandfather. So I was returning to my ancestral homeland actually.
segments.textZh: 所以我会做个简要讲述，因为到这个时候，故事已经变得有点长了。我大约17岁时来到北美。我出生在南非，但实际上，我的名字取自我的美国曾祖父。所以实际上，我是在回归自己的祖籍故土。

segments.textEn: And he was John Elon Haldeman and he was actually from Minnesota and generally from the Minnesota, Wisconsin area anyway. But I wanted to come to the United States because I think it's where great things are possible. It's where the technological frontiers are pushed forward. And I knew I wanted to be involved in that. I didn't know exactly how, but anyway, I went through college and ended up eventually at Stanford with the idea of studying applied physics and material science, trying to figure out ways to store energy more effectively for electric cars so you can make them go further.
segments.textZh: 他叫约翰·埃隆·霍尔德曼，实际上来自明尼苏达州，总之大体来自明尼苏达州、威斯康星州一带。但我想来美国，因为我认为这里能成就伟大的事情。这里推动着技术前沿不断向前发展。我知道自己想参与其中。我并不确切知道该怎么做，但无论如何，我读完了大学，最终去了斯坦福，打算学习应用物理学和材料科学，试图找出为电动汽车更有效地储存能量的方法，让它们能够行驶得更远。

segments.textEn: And I ended up putting that on hold to start an Internet company in 95. And at the time it wasn't from the perspective of making a lot of money because nobody had made any money on the Internet in 95. But it seemed to me that the Internet was something that would create effectively like a nervous system for Humanity. So whereas previously if you wanted to access information, you'd have to go to a library. And you know, even if you went to a lot of libraries, you still wouldn't have access to all that much information.
segments.textZh: 后来我暂停了那件事，在95年创办了一家互联网公司。当时并不是出于赚很多钱的考虑，因为95年还没有任何人在互联网上赚到钱。但在我看来，互联网会创造出一种实际上类似于人类神经系统的东西。所以在此之前，如果你想获取信息，就得去图书馆。而且你知道，即便你去了很多图书馆，仍然无法获取太多信息。

segments.textEn: But if everything got connected, then anyone, anywhere, if you were in sort of a jungle in middle of Amazon jungle in South America or something, and you had an Internet connection, you'd have access to all the world's information. In fact, you'd have access to more information than the US president did in, let's say, 1980.
segments.textZh: 但如果一切都连接起来，那么任何地方的任何人，比如说，如果你身处南美洲亚马孙雨林中央之类的地方，只要有互联网连接，就能获取全世界的信息。事实上，你能获取的信息会比，比如说，1980年的美国总统还多。

segments.textEn: So it'd be pretty incredible and transformative. So I thought, well, I wanted to be part of helping make that happen. And so I decided to put my studies at Stanford on hold and started an Internet company initially to help the media companies get online. And so we had as investors and customers, New York Times company, Post Niter and so forth. And that ended up working out. So we sold that company and then created PayPal.
segments.textZh: 所以这会非常不可思议，并带来变革。所以我想，好吧，我希望能参与其中，帮助促成这件事。因此，我决定暂停在斯坦福的学业，创办了一家互联网公司，最初是为了帮助媒体公司上线。我们的投资者和客户包括《纽约时报》公司、波斯特·奈特等。最后进展很顺利。于是我们卖掉了那家公司，然后创立了PayPal。

segments.textEn: And the idea behind PayPal was simply to facilitate payments on the Internet, because at the time, if you bought something from someone, you'd have to mail them a check and it would take weeks to conduct the transfer. We figured out how to make it really fast and easy to transfer funds from one person to another. And that actually grew super fast. It grew virally. And the key to that was figuring out how to make the friction of signing up for an account very, very low and make it easy for one person to refer another.
segments.textZh: PayPal背后的想法很简单，就是促进互联网上的支付，因为当时如果你从某人那里买东西，就得给对方邮寄一张支票，完成转账需要几周时间。我们找出了让资金从一个人转给另一个人变得真正快速而简便的方法。它实际上增长得极快。它呈病毒式增长。而关键在于找出如何把注册账户的阻力降得非常、非常低，并让一个人能够轻松推荐另一个人。

segments.textEn: And so as our customer base grew, the actual rate of growth grew. And this resulted in some initial challenges in scaling because we started off with five people in customer service. And after two months we had 100,000 customers.
segments.textZh: 所以随着我们的客户群增长，实际增长速度也在提高。这在扩展规模方面带来了一些初期挑战，因为我们的客户服务团队一开始只有5个人。2个月后，我们就有了100,000名客户。

segments.textEn: So our phone lines exploded, basically. But we're able to overcome those issues.
segments.textZh: 所以我们的电话线路基本上被打爆了。但我们得以克服那些问题。

segments.textEn: And then ebay bought the company in 2002, and it's sort of growing from there.
segments.textZh: 然后eBay在2002年收购了这家公司，此后它算是一直发展至今。

segments.textEn: So what that did though, was gave me the capital to try to do some things that are fairly high capital. And there were two things. There are two areas that I really wanted to get into. One was sustainable energy production and consumption of energy in a sustainable manner. And the other was space exploration. And I started off initially with the idea of doing something in the space exploration arena.
segments.textZh: 不过，这件事带来的结果是，它给了我资本去尝试做一些相当需要资本的事情。有两件事。有两个领域是我真正想进入的。一个是可持续能源生产，以及以可持续方式消耗能源。另一个是太空探索。我最初是从在太空探索领域做些事情的想法开始的。

segments.textEn: In fact, it wasn't actually with the idea of creating a company. It was initially with the thought of spurring interest in sending people to Mars. So I put together this idea of called Mars Oasis, which was to send a small greenhouse to the surface of Mars and get people excited about the idea of going there and thus increase NASA's budget in order to make it happen. As I got more and more into that, I discovered that the real issue was that the cost of space transportation was really high, in fact and it was getting worse.
segments.textZh: 事实上，当时其实并没有创办一家公司的想法。最初的念头是激发人们对把人送上火星的兴趣。于是我构想了一个叫作“火星绿洲”的方案，就是把一座小型温室送到火星表面，让人们对前往那里这个想法感到兴奋，从而增加NASA的预算，以实现这件事。随着我越来越深入地参与其中，我发现真正的问题在于太空运输成本非常高，事实上还在变得更糟。

segments.textEn: So we're used to technology getting better every year, but in some arenas it actually does not. It goes gets worse. Particularly when you consider that in 1969 we were able to go to the moon and then we're unable to go beyond low Earth orbit. And now with the space shuttle retired, we're not even able to go to Earth orbit at all, even with people. So that's, you know, that was not the right trajectory.
segments.textZh: 所以我们习惯了技术每年都会进步，但在某些领域，实际上并非如此。它会变得更糟。尤其是考虑到1969年我们还能登上月球，之后却无法飞越近地轨道。而现在随着航天飞机退役，我们甚至根本无法进入地球轨道，即使载人也不行。所以那，你知道，那并不是正确的发展轨迹。

segments.textEn: So I actually went to Russia three times to look at buying an ICBM to launch this mission.
segments.textZh: 所以我实际上去了俄罗斯3次，考虑购买一枚洲际弹道导弹来发射这项任务。

segments.textEn: Just very crazy,
segments.textZh: 就是非常疯狂，

segments.textEn: very cool.
segments.textZh: 非常酷。

segments.textEn: So after my third trip of trying to negotiate with the Russians to buy an ICBM and I did actually get a deal so figured out what it would cost and everything. But I concluded that my initial assumption had been wrong, that it was not a question of trying to generate more world to explore. Because I think the United States in particular is distillation of the human spirit of exploration people, it's face exploration is fundamental to the American psyche.
segments.textZh: 所以在我第3次前往俄罗斯、试图就购买一枚洲际弹道导弹进行谈判之后，我实际上确实谈成了一笔交易，也弄清楚了它的成本以及一切。但我得出结论，我最初的假设是错的，问题并不在于试图创造更多可供探索的世界。因为我认为，尤其是美国，是探索人们的人类探索精神的凝练，它的面部探索是美国心理的根本组成部分。

segments.textEn: But people really need to believe that it can be done and it's not going to break the bank if it does. So that's when I decided to start a rocket company.
segments.textZh: 但人们确实需要相信这件事能够做到，而且即便去做，也不会花到倾家荡产。所以就是在那时，我决定创办一家火箭公司。

segments.textEn: And I actually didn't think it would succeed and it almost didn't. So we started off developing a small rocket which was kind of a scale model version. It was about £100,000 of thrust. So big, you know, big by normal standards, but small for a rocket. And developed the engine and the airframe and the electronics and the guidance control system and then proceeded to have three failed launches in a row.
segments.textZh: 而且我其实不认为它会成功，它也差一点就没成功。所以我们一开始研发的是一枚小型火箭，算是一种按比例缩小的模型版本。它的推力约为£100,000。所以很大，你知道，按通常标准来说很大，但对火箭来说很小。我们研发了发动机、机身、电子设备和制导控制系统，随后连续进行了3次失败的发射。

segments.textEn: And so for various technical reasons, the first three launches did not succeed in reaching orbit. Launches two and three did get to space, but they didn't achieve enough speed to reach orbital velocity.
segments.textZh: 所以由于各种技术原因，前3次发射都没能成功进入轨道。第2次和第3次发射确实进入了太空，但没有达到足以实现轨道速度的速度。

segments.textEn: And so this is 2008 and so we're heading into the recession and we had one rocket left.
segments.textZh: 所以当时是2008年，我们正步入经济衰退，而我们只剩下1枚火箭。

segments.textEn: And unfortunately in late 2008 that fourth launch did work and we made it to orbit and then we won an asset contract after that. And so fortunately things worked out. But if that fourth launch had not worked, then SpaceX wouldn't be around. So it was very close call. In fact, when I started I thought, okay, I've got enough money, I think I've got enough money for three launches.
segments.textZh: 而不幸的是，在2008年末，第4次发射确实成功了，我们进入了轨道，之后又赢得了一份资产合同。所以幸运的是，事情最终进展顺利。但如果第4次发射没有成功，SpaceX就不会存在了。所以那真是千钧一发。事实上，我刚开始时想，好吧，我有足够的钱，我想我的钱足够进行3次发射。

segments.textEn: Unfortunately, it was just enough to make that fourth one.
segments.textZh: 不幸的是，钱刚好足够完成第4次发射。

segments.textEn: So in parallel there was, it was Tesla and the, the emphasis for Tesla was, was really to, to create a compelling electric car. And at first I thought there would, there would not really be a need for such a thing because I don't know if people are aware of this, but GM at the time had created the EV1 or Electric Vehicle 1 and Toyota done the electric RAV4. It been primarily as a result of regulations from the zero emission mandate states, particularly California.
segments.textZh: 所以与此同时，还有，Tesla，而Tesla的重点，确实是打造一款有吸引力的电动汽车。起初我以为并不会，实际上并不需要这样的东西，因为我不知道大家是否知道，但通用汽车当时已经制造了EV1，也就是电动汽车1，而丰田也制造了电动版RAV4。这主要是零排放强制规定州的法规所促成的，尤其是加利福尼亚州。

segments.textEn: So they created these electric vehicles and I thought, okay, this is great. Well, GMs obviously can go from the EV1 to the EV2 and EV3 and everything will be fine. But when California changed its regulations, they actually GM recalled all the EV1s and then crushed them so that they could never be returned. So it was clear that if a startup company did not create an electric vehicle and show that it's possible to have an electric car that looks good, goes fast, has long range, and that if you created such a thing that people would buy it, then it would be a very long time before the large incumbents did so.
segments.textZh: 所以他们制造了这些电动汽车，而我当时想，好吧，这很棒。嗯，通用汽车显然可以从EV1发展到EV2和EV3，一切都会顺利。但加利福尼亚州修改法规后，通用汽车实际上召回了所有EV1，然后将它们压毁，使它们永远无法再被归还。因此很明显，如果一家初创公司不制造电动汽车，不证明电动汽车可以外形美观、速度快、续航里程长，也不证明如果你造出这样的东西，人们就会购买，那么大型现有企业要这样做还会需要非常长的时间。

segments.textEn: And so that was the, I felt was important that we create Tesla for that reason.
segments.textZh: 所以那就是，我觉得出于那个原因，我们创立Tesla很重要。

segments.textEn: And Tesla also almost died in 2008.
segments.textZh: 而Tesla在2008年也差一点倒闭。

segments.textEn: And as you recall, the recession was particularly difficult for car companies. And right as in the summer of 2008, we had to raise a big funding round. But because of the collapse in the financial system, that funding round didn't happen. And we had to piece together the money to keep the company going from myself and existing investors. And we were able to just complete a financing round that was just barely enough to keep the company going.
segments.textZh: 你们应该还记得，那次经济衰退对汽车公司来说尤其艰难。就在2008年夏天，我们必须进行一轮大规模融资。但由于金融体系崩溃，那轮融资没有实现。我们不得不从我本人和现有投资者那里拼凑资金，让公司继续运营。我们勉强完成了一轮融资，金额刚刚够维持公司运转。

segments.textEn: And we closed it on the last hour of the last day that it was possible to do so.
segments.textZh: 而且，我们是在仍有可能完成此事的最后一天的最后一个小时完成交割的。

segments.textEn: It was Christmas Eve 2008, 6pm and after that the investors would have had, they were going on vacation, wouldn't have been possible to bring them back to the table, and we would have run out of money a few days after Christmas. So that was also a close call. So while things are going really well these days, I think it's always important to remember that when you're creating a company there are very dark times and it's about getting through those dark times.
segments.textZh: 当时是2008年平安夜下午6点，之后投资者本来就会，他们要去度假，不可能再把他们请回谈判桌，而我们会在圣诞节后几天耗尽资金。所以那次也是险象环生。因此，虽然这些日子事情进展得非常顺利，但我认为始终要记住，当你创办一家公司时，会有非常黑暗的时期，关键在于熬过那些黑暗时期。

segments.textEn: That's the difference between success and failure.
segments.textZh: 这就是成功与失败的区别。

segments.textEn: So of course now things are actually going pretty well for Tesla. May they stay that way. And also for SpaceX, we've got the Model S which is in production and it's the, it was like Consumer Reports gave it a 99 out of 100, which is actually the highest score that Consumer Reports has ever given a car of any kind was given to the Model S.
segments.textZh: 所以当然，现在Tesla的情况实际上相当不错。愿它们继续如此。SpaceX也是如此，我们有已经投产的Model S，而且它是，它就像《消费者报告》给了它99分（满分100分），这实际上是《消费者报告》有史以来给任何类型汽车打出的最高分，而这个分数给了Model S。

segments.textEn: And then when the federal government did the safety tests, it actually also got the highest safety rating of any car ever, including many vans and SUVs, so for a sedan.
segments.textZh: 然后，联邦政府进行安全测试时，它实际上也获得了有史以来所有汽车中的最高安全评级，其中包括许多厢式车和SUV，所以对于一辆轿车而言。

segments.textEn: And anyway, so that's going pretty well. And we're actually exporting a lot of the cars to Europe currently, and then we start exporting to Asia. And it's funny because I was wondering, we got these incredibly good rates for shipping goods to China because all these container ships come in full and they go back empty.
segments.textZh: 总之，这方面进展得相当顺利。我们目前实际上正向欧洲出口大量汽车，接下来会开始向亚洲出口。这很有意思，因为我当时在想，我们把货物运往中国的运费低得令人难以置信，因为所有这些集装箱船都是满载而来、空载返回。

segments.textEn: So it's real cheap to ship things to China.
segments.textZh: 所以把东西运到中国真的很便宜。

segments.textEn: So we'll start doing that in first quarter. And then with SpaceX, we've got a launch coming up which is our next generation rocket. Because the key thing for rocketry, the key breakthrough that's needed, is to create a fully reusable rocket. Because I think what SpaceX has done thus far is evolutionary but not revolutionary. In order for that to occur, you have to bring the rocket back to the launch pad and be able to relaunch it again.
segments.textZh: 所以我们将在第一季度开始这样做。然后在SpaceX这边，我们即将进行一次发射，使用的是我们的下一代火箭。因为对火箭技术来说，关键所在、所需的关键突破，是造出完全可重复使用的火箭。因为我认为SpaceX迄今所做的是渐进式的，而不是革命性的。要做到这一点，你必须让火箭返回发射台，并且能够再次发射。

segments.textEn: It has to be reusable, much in the way that an airplane or a car or any other mode of transport is reusable. So that's kind of the holy grail goal of spaceflight, which we're hoping to make progress towards, but it's very risky. So there's a good chance that the upcoming launch could go wrong. It's currently slated for the end of this month and hopefully that goes well. It's a tricky thing with rocket business because you can't issue a recall or, you know, send a software patch or anything after the rocket lifts off.
segments.textZh: 它必须能够重复使用，就像飞机、汽车或任何其他交通工具都能重复使用一样。所以，这算是太空飞行的圣杯目标，我们希望能在这方面取得进展，但风险非常高。因此，即将进行的发射很有可能出问题。目前计划在本月底进行，希望一切顺利。火箭业务有一个棘手之处，因为火箭升空后，你无法发布召回通知，或者，你知道，发送软件补丁之类的东西。

segments.textEn: Nine minutes later, it's either in orbit or it's exploded. So, yeah, it's nervous. Nine minutes.

segments.textZh: 是的，你好，我叫杰克逊。

segments.textEn: I'm a Sentinel high schooler from Missoula, Montana. Thank you for coming. And I want to know what is
segments.textZh: 我是蒙大拿州米苏拉市哨兵高中的一名学生。感谢您的到来。我想知道，什么是

segments.textEn: the one thing that has surprised you about your life?
segments.textZh: 您人生中让您感到意外的一件事？

segments.textEn: Oh, one thing. Wow. Well, I certainly, I'm surprised by the whole thing, honestly.
segments.textZh: 哦，一件事。哇。嗯，老实说，我当然对这一切都感到意外。

segments.textEn: I certainly didn't expect to for any of these things to happen. Honestly, Yeah, I just knew. I knew I wanted to be involved in technology.
segments.textZh: 我当然没料到这些事情中的任何一件会发生。老实说，是的，我只是知道。我知道我想参与科技。

segments.textEn: And in fact, the only reason I started a company back in 95, an Internet company, was because I couldn't get it. There were only a few Internet companies, and I couldn't get a job at any of them.
segments.textZh: 事实上，我之所以在95年创办一家公司，一家互联网公司，只是因为我没能如愿。当时只有几家互联网公司，而我在其中任何一家都找不到工作。

segments.textEn: I tried to get a job at Netscape and sent my resume in and tried hanging out in the lobby, but I was too shy to talk to anyone. And then I was like, okay, well, I guess I'll have to start a company because I can't get a job anywhere.
segments.textZh: 我试着去网景找工作，投了简历，还试着待在大堂里，但我太害羞了，不敢和任何人说话。然后我就想，好吧，看来我只好创办一家公司了，因为我到哪里都找不到工作。

segments.textEn: Thank you.
segments.textZh: 谢谢。

segments.textEn: My name is Toby McAdam. I have a company called Rising Sun Health. I deal with government regulations. What do you think of them? I actually. Dealing with the FDA, and after talking to Senator DeBauch, I've had 15, 15 attorneys, and they spent three and a half million dollars. We're in the middle of a consent.
segments.textZh: 我叫托比·麦克亚当。我有一家名为旭日健康的公司。我和政府监管打交道。您怎么看它们？我其实。和FDA打交道，而且在与德博参议员交谈后，我有过15名、15名律师，他们花了350万美元。我们正处于一项同意的中间。

segments.textEn: They have 15 attorneys. After I've talked to Senator Baucus and Senator Tester, we ended up with 15 attorneys on the FDA, and they've signed a consent decree. But government regulation, what do you think of those? Are they too strict? Because with the fda, they haven't had a reg. They haven't had a. I guess since 1995, but they keep changing the rules. And right now, in the last three years, more fatalities have been in the previous 50.
segments.textZh: 他们有15名律师。在我与鲍卡斯参议员和泰斯特参议员交谈后，我们最后有15名律师对付FDA，他们签署了一项同意令。但政府监管，您怎么看那些监管？它们是不是太严格了？因为就FDA而言，他们一直没有一项规。他们一直没有一项。我猜是自1995年以来，但他们不断改变规则。而现在，在过去3年里，更多的死亡事件发生在此前50个……

segments.textEn: Yeah, I mean, I think we probably are getting a bit too regulated, you know, how would you recommend going about it?
segments.textZh: 是的，我是说，我觉得我们受到的监管可能确实有点过多了，你知道，您建议怎么处理？

segments.textEn: Because I tried Senator Debauch and Senator Tester, and I just keep getting attorneys.
segments.textZh: 因为我找过德博参议员和泰斯特参议员，可我得到的总是律师。

segments.textEn: I actually had to file papers against the FDA myself.
segments.textZh: 我实际上不得不亲自提交针对FDA的文件。

segments.textEn: Right.
segments.textZh: 对。

segments.textEn: Well, I don't know. I think generally with laws and regulations, I think they should all come with some sort of a sunset clause, you know, because otherwise they have infinite life.
segments.textZh: 嗯，我不知道。我觉得一般来说，对于法律和法规，我认为它们都应该附带某种日落条款，你知道，因为否则它们的寿命就是无限的。

segments.textEn: Right. Do you think they should set standards where all companies follow?
segments.textZh: 对。您认为他们应该制定所有公司都遵循的标准吗？

segments.textEn: Well, I do think. I mean, I do think that there ought to be standards bodies. I'm not. I'm not completely libertarian in the sense of, like, I don't think there should be regulations at all. I just think that the natural bias of regulations is to last forever unless they're actively. I mean, you have to actively delete a regulation or a law, you know, the way things are set up in most laws. Some laws have sunset provisions.
segments.textZh: 嗯，我确实认为。我是说，我确实认为应该有标准机构。我并不。我并不是完全的自由意志主义者，也就是说，我并不认为完全不应该有监管。我只是认为，监管天然的倾向就是永远持续下去，除非有人主动。我是说，你必须主动删除一项法规或一部法律，你知道，大多数法律的设置方式就是这样。有些法律有日落条款。

segments.textEn: And the problem with that is you get vested interests who like that law, and there's an inertia around it. And so over time, the body of law and regulations grows and grows and grows. And I mean, it is something that I think is not ultimately good for society. So, in fact, I think it would generally be a good idea to have it such that it's hard to establish a rule and easy to remove one.
segments.textZh: 而问题在于，你会遇到喜欢那部法律的既得利益者，并且它周围存在一种惯性。因此随着时间推移，法律和法规的体量不断增长、不断增长、不断增长。而且我是说，我认为这件事最终对社会并无益处。所以事实上，我认为一般来说，让规则难以确立、易于废除会是个好主意。

segments.textEn: What you're saying is the rules should be consistently used to all, all companies?
segments.textZh: 您的意思是，规则应该一致地适用于所有、所有公司？

segments.textEn: Well, sure, of course, absolutely. That's. That's fair.
segments.textZh: 嗯，当然，当然，完全可以。这。这样很公平。

segments.textEn: Thank you.
segments.textZh: 谢谢。

segments.textEn: You're very welcome. One couple more, very quick. We're, we're already over the end.
segments.textZh: 非常不客气。再来一两个，很快。我们、我们已经超过结束时间了。

segments.textEn: There's a big sign here that says the end, by the way. It's just Craig Sundberg.
segments.textZh: 顺便说一句，这里有一块大牌子，上面写着“结束”。只是克雷格·桑德伯格。

segments.textEn: It's not the end.
segments.textZh: 还没结束。

segments.textEn: You know, I'm just. I'm just always been there.
segments.textZh: 你知道，我只是。我只是一直都在那里。

segments.textEn: Go ahead. Right here.
segments.textZh: 请说。就在这里。

segments.textEn: I just. I've been interested in space travel. I know one of the problems where they've had was the lack of gravity and effects of that on the human body. I was wondering how your company has made progress in that area so that, you know, colonization of Mars at some point can be possible.
segments.textZh: 我只是。我一直对太空旅行感兴趣。我知道他们遇到的一个问题是缺乏重力，以及这对人体的影响。我想知道贵公司在这方面取得了怎样的进展，从而让，你知道，在未来某个时候殖民火星成为可能。

segments.textEn: Sure. Well, the zero gravity on the way to Mars is not too much of a problem because people have actually shown that they can live for over a year in zero gravity. And, you know, your bones do get a little thinner, but they come back and they're walking around, they're doing fine. So I think the zero gravity trend, you know, spending three to six months in zero gravity is not a problem.
segments.textZh: 当然。嗯，前往火星途中处于零重力状态并不算太大的问题，因为人们实际上已经证明，他们可以在零重力环境中生活超过1年。而且，你知道，你的骨骼确实会变薄一点，但他们回来后也能四处走动，情况很好。所以我认为零重力这个趋势，你知道，在零重力环境中度过3到6个月不是问题。

segments.textEn: And then one can deal with the solar radiation, solar storms, essentially, by having a column of water between you and the sun. So on your spaceship, you orient the spaceship so that there's a column of water between you and the sun. That'll take care of the solar storms. Thank you.
segments.textZh: 然后，基本上，可以通过让你和太阳之间隔着一道水柱来应对太阳辐射、太阳风暴。所以在飞船上，你要调整飞船的朝向，让你和太阳之间隔着一道水柱。这样就能应对太阳风暴。谢谢。

segments.textEn: We're going to have to wrap up here. I'm really very Elon will tell you this sign. The end has been up for about 10 minutes.
segments.textZh: 我们得在这里结束了。我真的非常，埃隆会告诉你这块牌子。“结束”已经举了大约10分钟。

segments.textEn: Yeah.
segments.textZh: 对。
